posts.title: How we count a coach of 42 in under four minutes
posts.excerpt: A calm, consistent boarding routine allows four leaders to account for forty-two students before every coach departure without haste or confusion.
posts.content:
Every school trip involves moments of transition where distraction can easily lead to delay. Boarding a coach beside a busy roadside lay-by or outside a ferry terminal is often where group leaders feel the greatest anxiety. Over sixteen years and six hundred and twelve tours since Mara Lindqvist founded Tabidachi Study Tours in 2009, our team has refined a boarding process that removes urgency and guesswork. On Day three of our Year eight history trip along the Normandy coast, forty-two students and four leaders assembled by Coach two in Caen at eight fifteen. The entire headcount was completed and verified in three minutes and forty seconds.

The foundation of a rapid, accurate count is maintaining a strict ratio of one leader for every ten students, with school teachers counted alongside our tour team. For Coach two, this means Daniel Okafor and three accompanying staff know precisely which ten or eleven pupils they oversee. Rather than attempting to scan a moving crowd of forty-two teenagers, supervision is divided into four small clusters before anyone approaches the vehicle door. Each student knows their assigned leader and knows to assemble beside them as soon as luggage is loaded into the hold.

Positioning at the vehicle is fixed and predictable. Daniel stands at the open front door of the white coach wearing his navy gilet and lanyard, clipboard in hand. Beside him, the lead history teacher holds the printed master seat plan. The students do not board in an unstructured rush; they approach in single file by pre-arranged seat pairs. As each pupil steps through the door, Daniel marks the register with a quick visual check and raises his hand lightly to pace the line. No student is counted twice, and no student boards without eye contact.

Inside the coach, the second and third leaders are already positioned at the middle and rear rows. As students reach their designated seats, they immediately sit down and fasten their seatbelts. A seated group cannot wander or obscure other pupils, making visual verification straightforward. When the final student boards, the teacher calls out forty-two on and Daniel confirms forty-two counted. The driver verifies that the luggage bay is locked, and the vehicle is ready to depart for the morning workshop at Bayeux.

This disciplined routine occurs at least three times every day: during the morning breakfast count at seven thirty in the hostel, before departing Caen at eight fifteen, and when returning from the sea wall at Arromanches at seventeen forty. By anchoring the headcount to specific daily checkpoints, students internalise the pattern. They treat the roll call not as an interruption, but as an ordinary, comforting rhythm of travel. Teachers are spared the exhaustion of shouting names across parking bays, and the schedule proceeds without friction.

Discipline on the road is what makes educational travel enjoyable and safe. When headcounts are hurried or casual, mistakes happen and stress cascades through the entire teaching party. When headcounts are calm, methodical, and practiced, forty-two pupils board in under four minutes, leaving teachers free to focus on the day history lessons. By twenty-one hundred hours, when our evening message goes out to parents, every student has been counted, accounted for, and settled for journals before dinner.

posts.title: A risk assessment governors actually read
posts.excerpt: Two pages, one table and a plain sentence for every hazard: how we write assessments that are read, not filed.
posts.content:
A good assessment is short enough to be read at a governors’ meeting. Ours is two pages: the route and the sites on the left, the hazards in the middle, the controls and the named person on the right.

We visit every site before the proposal is finalised, and the assessment is signed in the spring term so that parents can see it at the parents’ evening.

posts.title: Packing for five nights: the list parents asked for
posts.excerpt: One bag, one pair of shoes you can walk in all day and a list that fits on a single page.
posts.content:
Parents asked for a list that fits on one page, so we wrote one. One cabin bag and one small rucksack, shoes that have already been walked in, a waterproof, a refillable bottle and the medicine in its original box with the dose written on it.

Everything else is already arranged: bed linen at the hostel, a packed lunch on travel days, and a leader who knows where every bag is.
